personalEssay.prompt: Reflect on a time when you questioned or challenged a belief or idea. What prompted your thinking? What was the outcome?
personalEssay.text:
In my family there is a saying that you never walk in front of your elders. Literally. If my grandfather is sitting on the couch and I need to get to the kitchen, I bend down low and say "tulou" as I pass, which means "excuse me," but also means "I know my place."

For most of my life, I thought my place was behind. Not in a sad way. In Tongan culture, respect for elders and for the family is everything, and I grew up loving that. Sunday dinners with forty cousins. Funerals that last a week, where everyone brings food and mats and money and nobody is ever left alone. My grandparents moved to Salt Lake City from Nukuʻalofa in 1989 with two suitcases, and they built a whole community here from scratch. I'm proud of that.

But somewhere in there I absorbed an idea that I didn't question until junior year: that being a good Tongan girl meant not taking up too much space. Don't be loud. Don't argue with adults. Don't leave.

What made me question it was, of all things, a college night. Junior year I helped start a Pacific Islander Student Union at my school, mostly because I noticed that the Polynesian kids all sat together at lunch but nobody ever talked to us about college. Our twenty members voted to host a college night, and we invited a Tongan professor from the University of Utah to speak.

I was in charge of introducing her. I practiced for days. When the night came, I stood up in front of about a hundred people, half of them aunties and uncles, and I froze. I had the speech on my phone and I couldn't read it. So instead I just said what was true. I said that I didn't know any Tongan woman who had a PhD until I googled one for this event, and that I wanted the little girls in the room to grow up knowing one.

The professor got up and hugged me. Then she told a story about her own father, who didn't want her to go to graduate school in California because it was too far away. She went anyway. He cried at her graduation. "Leaving isn't the opposite of respect," she said. "Sometimes it's how you bring something back."

I thought about that for weeks. The idea that ambition and family were opposites had felt so obviously true to me that I'd never even said it out loud. But the professor had done both. So had my grandparents, when you think about it. They left everything they knew, and that was an act of love for the family that came after them.

That changed how I talk to my own family. I used to stay quiet when my uncles said girls didn't need to go to college far away. Now I disagree, respectfully, but out loud. At first it caused some tension. My grandfather didn't talk to me for a full day after I told him I was applying out of state. But the next morning, he asked me to explain what a liberal arts college was. Then he asked me to explain it again to my grandmother.

I still say tulou when I walk in front of him. I don't think respect and ambition are enemies anymore. I think I can bend low and still go far.

supplements.prompt: Why are you interested in attending Pomona College?
supplements.text:
I want to go to Pomona because I want a college small enough that a girl from a big Tongan family won't feel lost, but far enough from home that I have to figure out who I am on my own.

When I visited, a student told me that professors at Pomona actually learn your name the first week, and I believed her, because one of them learned mine during a ten-minute info session. That matters to me. At my high school, I've had to fight a little to be noticed. As vice president of our Pacific Islander Student Union, I helped start a college night because nobody was talking to Polynesian students about college. I don't want to have to fight that hard for attention in college. I want to spend that energy learning.

I'm interested in studying anthropology and Asian American studies, and I love that Pomona's Asian American Resource Center includes Pacific Islander students in its programming. I'd want to get involved there right away, and also join a choir, because I can't imagine a week without singing.

The Claremont Colleges also mean I could take classes and find community across five campuses, which feels like the right balance for me: small but not tiny, close but not too close. My family will be a ten-hour drive away. That's far enough that I'll have to grow, and close enough that I can still make it home for the funerals and weddings that matter.
